job: Electric steering rack (rack and pinion) replacement
unit: per job: one steering rack / steering gear assembly (rack and pinion), fitted. All four examples have electric power steering (EPS), so the part is an electric rack; no hydraulic-rack example was built. Low = the lowest verified price for the assembly (aftermarket where one was found, otherwise the genuine part at an online discount), high = new genuine part at list (MSRP). Not included: the wheel alignment afterwards (see extras), outer tie rod ends, diagnosis, and power steering fluid on hydraulic systems

benchmarks.note: Acura RDX page: its one worked example, a 2018 RDX 3.5L V6 (an older model than our 2024 example), is $1,734.42 mobile and $2,115.30-$3,245.79 at a shop or dealer. benchmarks.name: Rick's Free Auto Repair Advice
benchmarks.note: named mechanic's guide (Rick Muscoplat, copyright 2017): 'can run between $900 and $2,200', dealer worked examples for 2009 cars with hydraulic racks (Dodge Grand Caravan $900, Toyota Camry V6 $2,025, Audi A4 $2,220); rebuilt aftermarket gears about $350-$800. Older than the others and for older, hydraulic-steering cars

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so there is nothing to call too wide or too narrow; this file is a first build. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2022 Honda Civic Touring about $2,003-$3,155 (1.9-3.5 hr); midsize 2013 Honda Accord 2.4L about $1,761-$3,173 (3.2-3.8 hr); truck 2019 Ram 1500 Classic about $1,967-$3,305 (1.3-3.5 hr); luxury 2024 Acura RDX about $2,478-$3,842 (1.5-3.5 hr). So about $1,750-$3,850 covers the four examples, and the part is 80 to 90 percent of every total. These totals fit the benchmarks for late-model cars: RepairPal's national average is $2,307-$2,572 and its Civic and Accord pages run $2,824-$3,178. IMPORTANT LIMIT: all four examples are recent vehicles with electric power steering, because those are the ones with a manufacturer-stated time. An older car with a hydraulic rack costs far less in parts: remanufactured hydraulic racks were seen at $106-$350 on the same retailer pages, and a mechanic's guide for 2009 cars gives $900-$2,200 at a dealer. No hydraulic example was built, so a range for the site should either say it is for electric racks or be widened downward (roughly $900 at the bottom) only after a hydraulic example is checked. How solid the labor times are: every low end is a manufacturer-stated time for the example vehicle itself (Honda 1.9 hr for the 2022-24 Civic, Honda 3.2 hr for the 2013-14 Accord L4, FCA 1.3 hr 4x4 / 1.4 hr 4x2 for the 2019 Ram 1500 Classic, Acura 1.5 hr for the 2024 RDX). All are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill, and all of them already include the alignment (the Ram time includes a toe set only), while this estimate treats the alignment charge as an extra; the labor was not reduced for that because no source splits it out. The midsize high end (3.8 hr) is Honda's own time for the V6 version of the same car. The high end for the other three classes (3.5 hr) rests on one general statement from a car-advice site, a weak source, supported only by Honda's 2.4-3.8 hr times for the CR-V and Accord; no shop book time was found for the Civic, Ram or RDX. Parts cautions: no aftermarket or remanufactured rack was found for the 2022 Civic or the 2024 RDX, so their low ends are the genuine part at an online discount; the Ram low end is also the discounted genuine part because the one aftermarket rack found (Dorman, $1,999.97, sold out) costs more; the Accord low end ($1,376.54) is a seller's own-brand rack whose page does not say new or remanufactured, and a $689 Duralo rack was seen sold out with no model years listed. The Civic has only one priced source for a new part (the second is a used rack, shown as a cross-check); the Civic recall bulletin names gearbox 53640-T21-305, which was not found in the parts catalog, so the catalog's Touring rack 53620-T22-A17 was priced instead. Rack prices vary a lot by trim: 2024 RDX racks list from $3,282 to $5,096 and Ram racks from $2,745 to $3,970. Confidence is low because of the single new-part source for the Civic, the missing aftermarket prices and the weak high-end time. This is an estimate, not a quote and not a diagnosis. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the general article's 3.5 hr is no longer a range end; the top for the Civic, Ram and RDX is Honda's 3.8 hr for the V6 Accord (a maker time, not the example vehicle). The Accord low is now the discounted genuine rack ($1,754.14) because the seller's own-brand rack at $1,376.54 does not state its condition. Built totals at $120-$160/hr: Civic about $2,003-$3,203, Accord $2,138-$3,173, Ram $1,967-$3,353, RDX $2,478-$3,890. This file covers electric racks only; older cars with hydraulic racks cost far less and are not covered.
extras: A quote nearly always adds a wheel alignment, which is not included here (the makers' warranty times above include it, or a toe set, in the labor). Also common: outer tie rod ends and their nuts, new mounting bolts the maker says not to reuse, a steering angle or stability-control sensor relearn or calibration on electric racks, a refundable core charge on a remanufactured rack, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. On hydraulic systems add power steering fluid, a system flush, and sometimes hoses or the pump if they contaminated or were contaminated by the old rack. If the subframe has to be lowered to get the rack out, labor rises and a full four-wheel alignment is needed. A rack replaced under a safety recall or warranty extension is done by the dealer at no charge, so check for open recalls first.
